check:0:0.q: Why not “The query: list prices are the real bill”?
check:0:0.a:
"The query: list prices are the real bill" gets one thing right. The query's math is sound. It takes each usage row, multiplies the DBUs (Databricks Units, the unit Databricks bills compute in) by the price for that SKU (the kind of compute), and adds it up under the `team` tag. If the tags are right, $4,000 is a fair picture of what team-ml used.

What it misses is what `system.billing.list_prices` actually holds. It is the **list price**: the public price per DBU. It knows nothing about the deal your company signed. Many companies agree a discount, for example by promising to spend a set amount over a year. The invoice uses that discounted price, so it comes out lower. Finance is not wrong. They are reading a different number.

So the $4,000 is a guide. It is good for comparing teams like team-ml and team-sales, or spotting a cluster that suddenly costs more. It is not the bill.

"Both: list price leaves out your discount" is better because it explains why the two numbers differ and why each one is correct for its own purpose.

judge.notes: No real problems. The example of a discount for a yearly spend commitment goes slightly beyond the lesson, but it is hedged with 'for example' and does not contradict it.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Finance: the system tables are often wrong”?
check:0:2.a:
That option gets one thing right. Finance's number is the one you actually pay, so their lower figure is real.

What it gets wrong is the reason. The system tables aren't broken. `system.billing.usage` records how many DBUs (Databricks Units, the unit compute is measured in) each team really used. For the `ml` team, those counts are accurate.

The gap comes from the price side. `system.billing.list_prices` holds the **list price**, the public price per DBU for each `sku_name`. It doesn't know about any discount your company agreed with Databricks or Microsoft. So the query multiplies correct DBUs by a price that's higher than yours. That gives a fair guide, but not the invoice.

Blaming the tables also leads you the wrong way. You might stop trusting tag-based reports. Yet they are still the best way to see who spent what, like `team-ml` versus `team-sales`, and how teams compare.

"Both: list price leaves out your discount" is better because it keeps the usage data and Finance's invoice both correct and names the real cause of the gap.

judge.notes: No real problems; the claim that tag reports are 'the best way' to see who spent what goes slightly beyond the lesson but does not contradict it.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Nothing: one DBU costs one dollar”?
check:1:0.a:
It gets one thing right. `usage_quantity` really is the amount you want to add up. It counts DBUs, short for Databricks Units, a measure of how much compute a job or cluster used.

What it misses is that a DBU has no single price. The price depends on the `sku_name`, which says what kind of compute was used. Jobs compute, all-purpose clusters and SQL warehouses each cost a different amount per DBU. Prices can also change over time, which is why the query matches on `price_start_time` and `price_end_time`.

Here is an example with made-up prices. Say `team-sales` burns 100 DBUs on `PREMIUM_JOBS_COMPUTE` at 0.30 a DBU. That is 30 dollars. Say `team-finance` burns 100 DBUs on an all-purpose cluster at 0.55 a DBU. That is 55 dollars. If you count one DBU as one dollar, both teams show 100 dollars. That is wrong for both, and it hides that finance spent almost twice as much.

"DBUs need multiplying by the SKU price" is the right answer. Only DBUs times the list price for that SKU turns usage into dollars you can compare between teams.

check:1:2.q: Why not “It should group by usage_date”?
check:1:2.a:
Grouping by `usage_date` would change the shape of the answer, not fix it. You would get a total per team per day instead of per team. That can be useful, for example to spot the day `team-sales` had a sudden jump. But each of those daily totals would still be DBUs, not dollars.

The real problem is the unit. `usage_quantity` counts DBUs (Databricks Units, a measure of how much compute was used). A DBU has no fixed dollar value. Its price depends on the `sku_name`, which says what kind of compute it was. So 40 DBUs of jobs compute and 40 DBUs of all-purpose compute can cost quite different amounts.

If you just add DBUs and call the result dollars, a team running cheaper compute looks as costly as one running pricier compute. Splitting by day does not change that. You would get the same wrong numbers, just cut into smaller pieces.

"DBUs need multiplying by the SKU price" is the better answer because it fixes the actual mistake: it turns usage into dollars before adding anything up.

check:2:0.q: Why not “A tag on every cluster”?
check:2:0.a:
A tag on every cluster is a good habit, but it does not answer the question.

**What it gets right.** A tag is a label, like `team = team-sales`, set on each cluster in `clusters.yml`. Databricks copies it into `custom_tags` on every row of `system.billing.usage`. That is how you know the spend is the sales team's and not someone else's. Without it, the money lands in "untagged" and nobody owns it.

**What it misses.** A tag only labels spend. It does not watch the total. It does not know about 2,000 dollars. It never sends an email. Your manager could tag every cluster perfectly and still get no alert when the team passes the limit.

So the tag is a helpful first step. It is not the thing that does the job.

**Why "A budget in the account console" is right:** a budget watches spend against the 2,000 dollar threshold you choose, filtered to a tag like `team = team-sales`, and emails your manager when spend passes it.

judge.notes: Minor: the claims that cluster tags flow into custom_tags and that a budget can filter by tag go slightly beyond the lesson text, but they do not contradict it.

check:2:1.q: Why not “A daily query you read by hand”?
check:2:1.a:
A daily query is not a bad idea. The SQL from this lesson really can show what `team-sales` spent this month. It joins `system.billing.usage` to `system.billing.list_prices` and adds up DBUs times price for that team's tag. So the numbers would be there.

What it misses is the actual ask. Your manager wants an **email** when spend passes 2,000 dollars. A query you read by hand sends nothing. It only works if someone remembers to run it and look every single day. People forget, go on holiday or skip a busy Friday. If spend jumps on Saturday, nobody knows until Monday.

It also puts the "is this over 2,000?" check in a person's head. That is the step most likely to slip.

A **budget** is a spend limit you set in the account console. The account console is the Databricks admin site that sits above all your workspaces, like DEV, UAT and PROD. The **threshold** is the dollar amount that triggers the alert.

A budget in the account console is better because it checks the 2,000-dollar threshold for you and sends the email automatically, with no one needing to remember.

judge.notes: Minor: the lesson's SQL covers the last 30 days at list price, not strictly 'this month', but this does not contradict the lesson.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Group and add up” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem.* "Our platform team runs Azure Databricks for many product teams. The bill shows up as one big number. Nobody can act on it until we can say whose spend it is."

*The idea.* "Each usage row has DBUs and a SKU. DBUs are Databricks Units, the billing unit. The SKU is the kind of compute, and it sets the price. I look up the list price for that SKU, multiply, and add the dollars to a running total for that row's `team` tag. It walks through the rows once."

*The edge case.* "Some rows have no `team` tag. I count them under 'untagged' instead of dropping them, so the totals still add up to the full spend. A big untagged pile is a warning sign. It means our Terraform defaults should put a `team` tag on every cluster, taken from team.yml."

**A likely follow-up**

"Will these numbers match the invoice?"

*Hint for a strong answer:* Say no. List price ignores any discount you have agreed, so treat it as a guide. Also mention that prices change over time. That is why the join picks the price that was valid when the usage started.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **A big "untagged" bucket.** If `untagged` is near the top, many clusters or jobs never got a `team` tag. Often the Service stage skipped adding the tag from `team.yml` to `clusters.yml` resources.
- **One team split in two.** You see `team-sales` and `Team-Sales` as separate rows. Tags match exactly, so casing or typos create extra groups.
- **Totals that look too high.** If a SKU's price changed during the month, a join without the time window matches each usage row to *both* prices. That row is counted twice.
- **A huge gap from the invoice.** Some gap is normal, because list price ignores discounts. A gap of several times is not.

**Quickest check**

Add up all DBUs for the last 30 days with no join. Then add them up again after the join. If the second number is bigger, rows are being duplicated.

Next, sum `list_dollars` across every team. Compare it with one total for all usage. The two should match.

Last, look at the share in `untagged`. In a healthy platform it stays small. It should shrink after each PROD apply that adds tags.

judge.notes: No major problem. The claim that a gap of several times from the invoice is abnormal goes beyond what the lesson says, but it is a reasonable rule of thumb.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three places where "join, multiply, group by tag" needs extra care.

**1. Tags are missing or inconsistent.** If `sp-sales-etl-dev` runs a job on a cluster with no `team` tag, that spend lands in "untagged." If one cluster says `team-sales` and another says `sales`, they count as two teams. The fix is to make Terraform add the `team` tag by default from each `team.yml`, and have Pydantic reject bad values before the Spacelift plan runs.

**2. You need the real bill, not a guide.** List price ignores any discount you have agreed. On classic compute, the Azure virtual machines are billed by Azure, not counted in DBUs (Databricks Units, the unit it bills compute in). For finance, compare against Azure Cost Management, which shows the full invoice.

**3. Many teams share one compute resource.** A shared SQL warehouse carries one set of tags, so all its spend goes to one team. Either give each team its own compute in `clusters.yml`, or split shared spend by who ran it, using the identity fields in `system.billing.usage`.

judge.notes: No real problems; the Azure VM billing and 'identity fields' points go beyond the lesson's text but are accurate and do not contradict it.

learn:term.a:
"List price" means the published price, before any deal.

Think of the sticker price on a car. Everyone sees the same number. But a company buying fifty cars might agree a lower price. The sticker is a fair guide, not what was actually paid.

Databricks works the same way. Each SKU has a public price per DBU. A SKU is a product code for one kind of compute, like `PREMIUM_JOBS_COMPUTE`. A DBU, or Databricks Unit, measures how much compute you used. Your organisation may have agreed a discount with Databricks or Microsoft, so the real invoice can be lower.

In the lesson's example, 0.30 a DBU is the list price. If `team-sales` ran 40 DBUs of jobs compute, the result shows 12.00 dollars. That means "what it would cost at the public rate."

In the SQL, the price comes from `p.pricing.default` in `system.billing.list_prices`. The query names its column `list_dollars` as a reminder of this.

Use these numbers to compare teams and spot fast growth. For the exact bill, check the invoice.

check:0:0.a:
"About $11" gets most of the maths right. It just stops one step too early.

Here is the working. A DBU (Databricks Unit) is the unit Databricks uses to measure compute use. You pay a price per DBU.

- 4 DBUs an hour at $0.55 each is $2.20 an hour.
- 5 idle hours a day at $2.20 is $11.

So $11 is the right cost for **one day** of idle time. The DBU rate and the idle hours are both used correctly.

What it misses is the time span. The question asks about 30 days. With `autotermination_minutes` set to 0, the cluster never stops by itself. So those 5 idle hours come back every day, and so does the $11. That gives $11 × 30 = $330.

This is the "quiet bill" the lesson warns about. One day looks small. A month is where the waste shows up. Picture a `team-sales` cluster left with auto-termination off in DEV. It could cost this much without anyone noticing.

"About $330" is better because it multiplies the daily idle cost by all 30 days, which is the period the question asks about.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Nothing, idle clusters are free”?
check:0:2.a:
"Nothing, idle clusters are free" gets one thing right: an idle cluster does no useful work. No job is running on it.

But it misses how billing works. A classic cluster bills for every minute it is running, busy or not. "Idle" just means running with nothing to do, so the meter keeps going. With auto-termination off (`autotermination_minutes = 0`), nothing stops it. All 5 idle hours each day get billed.

Picture team-sales asking for a cluster in their `clusters.yml` with `autotermination_minutes` set to 0. The lesson's `idle-limits` policy would block that, because it only allows 10 to 60. Without such a policy, every quiet evening costs money.

Here is the cost in words. Five idle hours a day for 30 days is 150 hours. At 4 DBUs an hour, that is 600 DBUs. A DBU (Databricks Unit) is how Databricks measures compute use. At $0.55 each, 600 DBUs comes to $330.

"About $330" is better because it treats idle minutes as billed minutes, which is exactly the quiet bill auto-termination exists to cap.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Straight away, because it's idle”?
check:1:0.a:
"Straight away, because it's idle" gets one thing right. Nobody is using the cluster, so it is doing no useful work. It would be nice if it stopped.

But a classic cluster does not stop just because it is idle. It keeps running, and billing, for every minute until something stops it. That "something" is normally **auto-termination**: a timer that shuts the cluster down after it has sat idle for `autotermination_minutes`.

Setting `autotermination_minutes` to `0` switches that timer off. So nothing will stop it automatically. Picture a `team-sales` cluster in `clusters.yml` with `0`. It could bill all weekend until someone in `grp-sales-dev-owners` stops it on Monday.

The "stops on its own quickly" idea fits serverless compute, not a classic cluster with `0`. This is also why the platform team uses a compute policy. A policy is a set of rules that limits what values people can choose. With a `minValue` of 10, nobody can pick `0` at all.

"Not until someone stops it" is better because `0` means auto-termination is off, so only a person (or a manual action) ends the billing.

check:1:1.q: Why not “After 60 minutes of idle time”?
check:1:1.a:
"After 60 minutes of idle time" gets one thing right. Auto-termination does stop a cluster after a stretch of idle time. Idle means running but doing no work. And 60 is a familiar number: it is the `maxValue` in the lesson's `idle-limits` policy.

But the question says `autotermination_minutes` is 0. For this setting, 0 is not a very short wait. **0 means "never auto-terminate."** Databricks does not quietly swap in a default like 60. The cluster keeps running, and billing, all weekend, until a person or a script stops it.

Picture team-sales asking for a cluster in `clusters.yml` with `autotermination_minutes: 0`. It is idle from Friday evening to Monday morning. That is about 60 hours of paid time doing nothing.

A policy could cap the value at 60. It does this by blocking 0, so nobody can choose 0 in the first place. It does not change what 0 means. The answer "after 60 minutes" would only be true if the cluster were set to 60.

"Not until someone stops it" is better because 0 turns auto-termination off, so nothing stops the cluster except a manual or scripted stop.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Send a reminder email each month”?
check:2:0.a:
A reminder email gets one thing right. It tells people why `autotermination_minutes = 0` is costly. Awareness helps.

But it misses the real problem. An email only asks. It can't stop anyone. Someone on team-sales writes a new cluster in `clusters.yml`, forgets the email, and sets `0` anyway. Spacelift plans and applies it. The cluster runs idle all night, and you pay for every minute. You only find out when the bill arrives. Then you send another email, and the cycle repeats. Reminders also fade. People skim them, and new team members never got last month's.

"For good" means the mistake can't happen, not just that it happens less often.

A compute policy is a set of rules attached to clusters. Databricks checks the rules whenever someone creates or edits a cluster. The lesson's `idle-limits` policy only allows `autotermination_minutes` between `10` and `60`. A cluster that uses the policy can't be set to `0`. Databricks rejects it.

Forcing a maximum in a compute policy is better because the platform enforces the limit on every cluster automatically, so nobody has to remember anything.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Switch everything off each night”?
check:2:2.a:
"Switch everything off each night" gets one thing right. A stopped cluster bills nothing, so a nightly shutdown does save some idle minutes.

But it misses the actual problem. The question is about people setting `autotermination_minutes` to 0. A nightly switch-off does not change that setting. During the day, a cluster set to 0 still sits idle and bills until the shutdown runs. And the next new cluster gets created with 0 again. You are cleaning up after the habit, not stopping it.

It also adds work. Someone has to build and look after that nightly job, which is a script on a timer. If it fails one night, those idle clusters keep billing and nothing catches them.

A compute policy is a set of rules that limits what a cluster's settings may be. In the lesson's `idle-limits` policy, `autotermination_minutes` has a `range` of 10 to 60. So a cluster created under that policy cannot be given 0.

Forcing a maximum in a compute policy is better because it blocks the bad setting when each cluster under that policy is created, so nobody has to clean up afterwards.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Cap each value, work out the cost, sort” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

*The problem.* "Teams like team-sales ask for clusters in `clusters.yml`. A classic cluster bills every minute it runs, even when nobody uses it. I want to know which clusters waste the most money sitting idle."

*The idea.* "For each cluster, I cap the idle time that gets billed. If `autotermination_minutes` is 0, the cluster never stops, so every idle minute counts. Otherwise it stops at its limit, so the bill can't go past that. Then I turn those minutes into money. I use DBUs, which are Databricks' unit for billing compute, and the price per DBU. Last, I sort with the most expensive first, so the worst cluster is easy to spot."

*The edge case.* "Zero looks like 'no idle time', but it means 'never stop'. Treat it like a small number and you hide the biggest bill."

**Likely follow-up**

"How would you stop a team setting 0 at all?"

*Hint:* Name two layers. First, a Pydantic rule in the config repo rejects 0 when the YAML is reviewed. Second, a `databricks_cluster_policy` with a range, such as 10 to 60, blocks 0 inside the workspace. That second layer also catches clusters created outside Terraform.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **Flat spend at quiet times.** A team's cost, say `team-sales` in DEV, stays steady overnight and on weekends, when no jobs run. Busy compute goes up and down. Idle compute just stays flat.
- **No idle stops in the event log.** Each cluster has an event log, a timeline of what happened to it. A healthy one often shows "terminated due to inactivity." If a cluster ran for days with no such entry, nothing is stopping it.
- **DEV costs close to PROD.** DEV sees light use, so its bill should be much smaller. If it isn't, idle clusters are a likely cause.
- **Suspicious settings in the Spacelift plan.** The plan shows `autotermination_minutes = 0`, or a very high value like 600. It also passes the policy checks. That usually means no compute policy is attached to that cluster.
- **A large `auto_stop_mins`** on a SQL warehouse.

**Quickest check**

List every cluster's `autotermination_minutes` from the Terraform plan or the workspace compute page. Treat any 0 as suspect, and look hard at any value over 60. Then confirm the cluster uses the `idle-limits` policy, which caps the value between 10 and 60.

judge.notes: The event-log 'terminated due to inactivity' point is not in the lesson, but it does not contradict it. The answer is about 190 words, close to the limit.

learn:stops.a:
**When the simple idle rule needs extra care**

**1. Idle time comes in many short gaps.**
The rule assumes one long idle stretch a day. Real use is often bursty. Say `team-sales` runs a notebook every 20 minutes on a cluster set to 30. It never stops, so every gap is billed in full. Look at real usage in the Databricks billing system tables instead of guessing one idle block.

**2. DBUs are not the whole bill.**
A DBU (Databricks Unit) is Databricks' own billing unit. On classic clusters, Azure also bills separately for the virtual machines underneath. So DBUs times price undercounts the real cost. Add the Azure VM cost for each `node_type_id`, or use serverless, where that cost is folded into the DBU price.

**3. The limit is set too low.**
A tiny `autotermination_minutes` saves idle cost. But each restart takes several minutes, and those minutes bill too. Analysts in `grp-sales-dev-owners` may restart all day. For short, frequent work, consider serverless compute or instance pools (ready-to-use spare machines that make startup faster). Keep your policy range sensible.

learn:term.a:
**Auto-termination** is an idle timer. It switches a cluster off when nobody has used it for a set time.

Think of a motion-sensor light in an office corridor. If no one walks past for a while, it turns itself off. Without the sensor, the light burns all night, and you pay for it.

A classic cluster is like that light. It bills for every minute it runs, busy or idle. `autotermination_minutes` is the timer: how many idle minutes to wait before stopping. Setting it to `0` removes the timer, so the cluster runs until a person stops it.

In the lesson's example:
- 300 idle minutes, `autotermination_minutes = 0`: the cluster never stops, so all 300 minutes are billed.
- 240 idle minutes, `autotermination_minutes = 30`: it stops after 30 idle minutes, so only 30 are billed.

In the Terraform, the `shared-analytics` cluster sets `autotermination_minutes = 30`. The `idle-limits` policy is a set of rules that forces a value between 10 and 60. So team-sales can't request `0` in their `clusters.yml`. SQL warehouses use the same idea, called `auto_stop_mins`.

judge.notes: No major problem. The only stretch is that it assumes team-sales uses the idle-limits policy, which the lesson never says.

check:0:0.a:
"Serverless compute" gets one thing right. A nightly job is the kind of work serverless often handles well. It starts in seconds, and nobody has to pick machine sizes.

But this job has a special need. It needs an **init script**: a small script that runs on each machine as it starts, here to install a company certificate. Serverless doesn't accept init scripts or any other custom machine setup. Databricks runs those machines for you, so you can't change how they boot. The certificate would never get installed, and the job would likely fail when it tries to connect to anything that needs it.

The special need decides the compute, not just the fact that it's a job. That is why the `nightly_load` job in the platform team's Terraform uses a `new_cluster` with an `init_scripts` block pointing at `/Shared/init/certs.sh`.

**Jobs compute** is better because it is classic compute that does run init scripts. It is also created just for each run and shut down afterwards, at a lower price per DBU than all-purpose compute.

judge.notes: Passes. Minor: the 'job would likely fail' consequence goes slightly beyond the lesson, and the Jobs compute part runs two sentences where one was asked.

check:0:2.a:
A SQL warehouse is a real Databricks compute choice. It is also the recommended home for SQL work, especially in its serverless form. So the instinct to pick a managed, ready-made option is reasonable.

The miss is the kind of work. The lesson's rules ask one question first: is it SQL? A SQL warehouse runs SQL, dashboards and Genie (plain-word questions about your data). A nightly job, such as one `team-sales` asks for to load data, is a job, not SQL work. So the SQL warehouse rule never applies here.

The next rule is the one that fits. The job needs an init script, which is a script that sets up each machine as it starts, here to install a company certificate. Work with an init script goes to classic compute, meaning machines in your own cloud account that you size yourself. For a job, that means jobs compute. You can see this in the lesson's `nightly_load` example: the `init_scripts` block sits inside its `new_cluster`.

Jobs compute is better because it is classic compute built for one job run, so it takes the init script, shuts down when the run ends, and costs less per DBU than all-purpose.

judge.notes: No real problems. Minor: it calls `nightly_load` "the lesson's" example when it is from the learner's Terraform stack, and "per DBU" is not re-explained.

check:1:1.a:
All-purpose compute isn't wrong in spirit. It's a real cluster, and it's built for people working by hand, the way an analyst does. So the instinct to pick something interactive makes sense.

But it misses two things.

**First, it isn't the tool made for this work.** In the lesson, the compute that runs SQL, dashboards and Genie is a SQL warehouse. All-purpose compute is for working in notebooks. A sales dashboard plus Genie questions is exactly the work a SQL warehouse is for.

There's no GPU and no init script, the setup script that runs as each machine starts.

The rule order says the same thing. Is it SQL? Then a SQL warehouse, whatever else it needs.

A serverless SQL warehouse is better because it's built for dashboards and Genie, and Databricks runs the machines for you, so it starts in seconds with nothing to size.

check:1:2.a:

The lesson's rule order says the same thing. The first question is "Is it SQL?" Dashboards and Genie are SQL work, so the SQL warehouse rule fits first and decides.

check:2:0.a:
